fracture-fatigue-001.question: The theoretical strength of a perfect crystal is estimated at roughly one tenth of the Young's modulus, yet the actual fracture strength of brittle materials such as glass is often only a few tens to a few hundreds of times smaller than that. What is the main reason?
choices: In real materials, the bonding force between the atoms themselves is only a few percent of the value assumed in the theoretical estimate
Stress concentrates at the tips of tiny cracks inside the material or on its surface, locally reaching the theoretical strength
The cross-sectional area shrinks under load, so the true stress becomes tens of times the nominal stress and reaches the theoretical strength
fracture-fatigue-001.explanation: The theoretical strength is the stress needed to pull planes of atoms apart all at once, on the order of E/10 (about 7 GPa for glass). Griffith proposed that real materials contain tiny cracks, and because stress concentrates at their tips and locally reaches the theoretical strength, fracture can start even when the average stress is far lower. The fact that freshly drawn glass fibers with flawless surfaces reach strengths of several GPa supports this idea. The bonding force itself is already built into the estimate of the theoretical strength, so it is not smaller than assumed. The difference between true and nominal stress concerns ductile materials that neck, and does not explain the low strength of brittle materials.

fracture-fatigue-002.question: An elliptical hole in a wide plate (radius along the major axis a = 1.0 mm, radius of curvature at the end of the major axis ρ = 0.040 mm) carries a tensile stress of 100 MPa perpendicular to the major axis. Estimating the maximum stress at the end of the hole with σmax = σ₀(1 + 2√(a/ρ)), which value is closest?
choices: About 1100 MPa
About 5100 MPa
About 140 MPa
fracture-fatigue-002.explanation: a/ρ = 1.0/0.040 = 25, so √(a/ρ) = 5, the stress concentration factor is Kt = 1 + 2×5 = 11, and the maximum stress is σmax = 100×11 = about 1100 MPa. The longer the hole and the sharper its end (the smaller ρ), the more the stress concentrates; when ρ shrinks to about an interatomic distance, as at a crack, the stress at the end reaches the theoretical strength even under a low average stress. About 5100 MPa skips the square root and uses 1 + 2a/ρ, and about 140 MPa swaps a and ρ to use √(ρ/a). For a circular hole (a = ρ), Kt = 3, and the formula also shows why rounding the root of a notch eases the stress concentration.

fracture-fatigue-003.question: A glass (Young's modulus E = 70 GPa, surface energy γs = 1.0 J/m²) has a surface crack of length a = 1.0 µm. Which value is closest to the fracture stress estimated with the Griffith equation σf = √(2Eγs/(πa))?
choices: About 149 MPa
About 374 MPa
About 211 MPa
fracture-fatigue-003.explanation: 2Eγs/(πa) = 2×70×10⁹×1.0/(3.14×1.0×10⁻⁶) ≈ 4.46×10¹⁶ Pa², and its square root is about 2.11×10⁸ Pa, or about 211 MPa. The Griffith equation comes from the condition that a crack grows unstably when the elastic strain energy released as it extends exceeds the energy 2γs of the two new surfaces it creates. About 149 MPa drops the factor of 2 that comes from forming two surfaces, and about 374 MPa forgets to divide by π. Because σf is inversely proportional to √a, making the crack 4 times longer halves the fracture stress.

fracture-fatigue-004.question: Among the modes of crack deformation, which statement correctly describes Mode I?
choices: The crack faces slide over each other in the direction of crack growth, an in-plane shear mode
The crack faces slide parallel to the crack front, an out-of-plane shear mode
The crack faces are pulled apart by tension perpendicular to them, an opening mode
fracture-fatigue-004.explanation: Crack deformation is divided into three modes: Mode I (opening), which pulls the crack faces apart; Mode II (in-plane shear), in which the faces slide in the direction of crack growth; and Mode III (out-of-plane shear), in which they slide parallel to the crack front. The stress intensity factors are likewise written K_I, K_II and K_III. Brittle materials break most easily under Mode I loading, and cracks tend to turn toward the direction that makes them Mode I, so fracture toughness is usually expressed as the critical value for Mode I, K_IC. Sliding in the direction of crack growth is Mode II and sliding parallel to the front is Mode III; these matter for cases such as cracks in shafts under torsion.

fracture-fatigue-005.question: In a ductile metal such as steel, the energy needed for a crack to advance (the critical energy release rate G_c) is orders of magnitude larger than 2γs (a few J/m²) estimated from the surface energy. What is the main reason?
choices: Plastic deformation occurs at the crack tip, and a large amount of energy is consumed as plastic work
The surface energy of metals is thousands of times larger than that of ceramics
Metals contain almost no cracks, so Griffith's idea does not apply to them
fracture-fatigue-005.explanation: Orowan and Irwin extended Griffith's idea to metals and wrote the energy needed for a crack to advance as G_c = 2γs + γp. Here γp is the plastic work consumed in the plastic zone at the crack tip; in ductile steels it exceeds 10⁴ J/m², far larger than 2γs. The surface energy of metals is roughly 1–3 J/m², not different from that of ceramics by orders of magnitude. Metals also contain inclusions and cracks, and Griffith's energy balance is still used as the foundation, with the plastic work added. In materials that hardly deform plastically, such as glass, G_c is a small value of the same order as 2γs.

fracture-fatigue-006.question: In a steel with a yield stress of 500 MPa, the stress intensity factor at a crack tip is K = 30 MPa·√m. Estimating the size of the plane-stress plastic zone (its distance from the crack tip) with r_p = (1/2π)(K/σy)², which value is closest?
choices: About 3.6 mm
About 0.57 mm
About 9.5 mm
fracture-fatigue-006.explanation: K/σy = 30/500 = 0.060 √m, which squared gives 3.6×10⁻³ m; dividing by 2π ≈ 6.28 gives r_p ≈ 5.7×10⁻⁴ m, about 0.57 mm. In the elastic solution, the stress at the crack tip grows without limit in proportion to 1/√r, but in reality the region where it exceeds the yield stress becomes a plastic zone, whose size is proportional to (K/σy)². About 3.6 mm forgets to divide by 2π, and about 9.5 mm skips the squaring and treats 0.060/2π as a length. Linear elastic fracture mechanics, which judges fracture by K, can be used when the plastic zone is much smaller than the crack length and the plate thickness. Under plane strain, the plastic zone is about one third of this value.

fracture-fatigue-007.question: Which pairing of a feature seen when observing a fracture surface in a scanning electron microscope with the type of fracture is correct?
choices: A fracture surface covered with many small hollows (dimples) indicates ductile fracture by the nucleation and coalescence of voids
A fracture surface that broke along flat crystal planes and shows river patterns indicates ductile fracture accompanied by extensive plastic deformation
A fracture surface on which the shapes of the grains stand out as they are indicates cleavage fracture that ran through the grains (transgranular fracture)
fracture-fatigue-007.explanation: In ductile fracture, voids form around inclusions and precipitates, then grow and coalesce, so the fracture surface is covered with many hollows (dimples). Cleavage fracture is a brittle fracture that splits through the grains along specific crystal planes; its surface is flat and shows river patterns, where steps merge like streams flowing together. Calling this ductile fracture gets it backwards. A fracture surface on which the grain shapes stand out like piled stones is intergranular fracture along grain boundaries, caused by temper embrittlement, hydrogen embrittlement, precipitation at grain boundaries and so on. Observing fracture surfaces (fractography) is the basis of failure analysis to find the cause of an accident.

fracture-fatigue-008.question: Which statement correctly describes the initiation of fatigue cracks when a stress amplitude below the yield stress is repeatedly applied to a metal with a smooth surface?
choices: The surface is protected by its oxide film, so fatigue cracks almost always start inside the material near its center
Below the yield stress, dislocations do not move at all, so no cracks form and the material lasts indefinitely
Localized slip repeats in grains near the surface, and surface intrusions and extrusions become the starting points
fracture-fatigue-008.explanation: Even at a stress amplitude below the yield stress, localized slip occurs in favorably oriented grains near the surface, and with repetition persistent slip bands form. Slip does not fully reverse even when it goes back and forth, so tiny irregularities called intrusions and extrusions appear on the surface, and these act as notches where cracks start. The surface is less constrained, carries scratches and corrosion, and in bending or torsion bears the highest stress, so most fatigue cracks start at the surface. Initiation from the interior is limited to cases such as inclusions acting as origins in high-strength steels in the very-high-cycle regime. Dislocations do not stay completely still, so fatigue failure occurs even below the yield stress.

fracture-fatigue-009.question: The fracture surface of a part that failed by fatigue shows shell-like patterns visible to the naked eye (beach marks) and fine lines visible in an electron microscope (striations). Which statement about them is correct?
choices: Both form one line per load cycle, so counting them gives the number of cycles to failure
Striations roughly mark the crack advance in each cycle, while beach marks record history such as shutdowns
Both form in the final fracture zone that broke all at once, gathering at the place farthest from the origin
fracture-fatigue-009.explanation: Striations are lines left as the crack tip opens and blunts, then closes and sharpens again in each cycle, and their spacing corresponds roughly to the crack growth per cycle, da/dN. The spacing is fine, at the µm level or below, and cannot be seen without an electron microscope. Beach marks are patterns that record positions of the crack front through shutdowns and restarts, changes in load level, differences in how corrosion progresses and so on, and each band contains many cycles. Both appear in the region where the fatigue crack advanced little by little, and the common center of the patterns shows the origin. The final fracture zone is where the remaining cross-section broke all at once, and it shows a ductile or brittle fracture surface.

fracture-fatigue-010.question: A cyclic stress with a mean stress σm = 200 MPa is applied to a steel with a fully reversed fatigue limit σw = 300 MPa and a tensile strength σB = 800 MPa. Using the modified Goodman relation σa = σw(1 − σm/σB), which value is closest to the stress amplitude corresponding to the fatigue limit?
choices: About 281 MPa
About 225 MPa
About 100 MPa
fracture-fatigue-010.explanation: σm/σB = 200/800 = 0.25, so σa = 300×(1 − 0.25) = 225 MPa. A tensile mean stress acts to open cracks, so the allowable stress amplitude is smaller than the fully reversed value (σm = 0). The modified Goodman diagram is a conservative guide that joins σw on the vertical axis and σB on the horizontal axis with a straight line. About 281 MPa is the value from the parabolic Gerber relation, which squares the mean stress ratio, 300×(1 − 0.25²), and is a less conservative estimate than Goodman. About 100 MPa divides by σw instead of σB. A compressive mean stress often works in favor of fatigue resistance, but designs usually do not take credit for that effect.

fracture-fatigue-011.question: Which surface treatment can be expected to improve the fatigue strength of a steel part?
choices: Finishing the surface rough so that paint and lubricants adhere to it more easily
Grinding the surface so that tensile residual stress remains in the surface layer
Introducing compressive residual stress into the surface layer by shot peening
fracture-fatigue-011.explanation: Most fatigue cracks start at the surface and open and grow under tensile stress. Shot peening fires small steel balls or similar media at the surface at high speed, plastically deforming the surface layer and leaving compressive residual stress; this offsets the tensile stress at the surface and suppresses crack initiation and early growth. Carburizing, nitriding and induction hardening also harden the surface layer and introduce compressive residual stress, so they raise fatigue strength. Surface roughness acts as small notches, so a rough finish lowers fatigue strength. Tensile residual stress is equivalent to shifting the mean stress toward tension and is harmful in fatigue. Poor grinding conditions can leave tensile residual stress in the surface layer.

fracture-fatigue-012.question: A steel part fails by fatigue after 1.0×10⁵ cycles at stress amplitude σ₁ and after 1.0×10⁶ cycles at σ₂. After it is used for 4.0×10⁴ cycles at σ₁, it continues to be used at σ₂. Which value is closest to the remaining life estimated with Miner's rule (failure when Σn/N = 1)?
choices: About 6.0×10⁵ cycles
About 9.6×10⁵ cycles
About 6.0×10⁴ cycles
fracture-fatigue-012.explanation: The damage at σ₁ is n₁/N₁ = 4.0×10⁴/1.0×10⁵ = 0.40, leaving 1 − 0.40 = 0.60. At σ₂, the damage per cycle is 1/N₂, so the remaining number of cycles is 0.60×1.0×10⁶ = 6.0×10⁵ cycles. About 9.6×10⁵ cycles subtracts the number of cycles itself, rather than the fraction of damage, from N₂, ignoring that the weight of one cycle differs with stress. About 6.0×10⁴ cycles multiplies the remaining fraction by the life N₁ at σ₁. Miner's rule is simple, but it cannot represent the effect of load sequence, and it is known that when the stress steps from high to low, the actual life tends to be shorter than estimated.

fracture-fatigue-013.question: Which statement about low-cycle fatigue (roughly 10⁴ cycles or fewer to failure) is correct?
choices: The basic approach is to rate it with stresses in the elastic range at a constant stress amplitude
With so few cycles, no fatigue cracks form, and failure is the same ductile fracture as from a single overload
Plastic strain occurs in every cycle, and the relation between plastic strain amplitude and life is expressed by the Coffin–Manson law
fracture-fatigue-013.explanation: In low-cycle fatigue, large plastic deformation is repeated in every cycle, and the plastic strain amplitude, rather than the stress, governs the life. It is therefore rated in tests at a constant strain amplitude, and the relation between the plastic strain amplitude Δεp/2 and the number of reversals to failure 2Nf is expressed as Δεp/2 = εf′(2Nf)ᶜ (c is about −0.5 to −0.7), a straight line on log-log axes. This is the Coffin–Manson law. Rating by stress amplitudes in the elastic range is the method of high-cycle fatigue, which uses S-N curves and Basquin's law. Low-cycle fatigue also ends in failure through crack initiation and growth, and it is a problem in power plants that start and stop repeatedly and in parts subject to thermal strain.

fracture-fatigue-014.question: Which statement correctly describes the curve of fatigue crack growth rate da/dN plotted against the stress intensity factor range ΔK on log-log axes?
choices: The middle region is a straight line given by the Paris law da/dN = C(ΔK)ᵐ, and below ΔK_th the crack hardly grows
da/dN is constant regardless of ΔK, set only by the crack length and the material's yield stress
The slope of the line decreases as ΔK grows, and crack growth stops when the maximum stress intensity factor approaches K_IC
fracture-fatigue-014.explanation: The curve is usually divided into three regions. In the low region where ΔK approaches the threshold ΔK_th, the growth rate drops sharply, and below ΔK_th the crack effectively does not grow. The intermediate region is a straight line on log-log axes and can be described by the Paris law da/dN = C(ΔK)ᵐ, with an exponent m of roughly 2–4 for metals. In the high region where the maximum stress intensity factor K_max approaches the fracture toughness K_IC, the rate rises sharply and leads to unstable fracture, so the claim that growth stops is backwards. ΔK = YΔσ√(πa) depends on both the stress range and the crack length, so the rate is not determined by crack length alone.

fracture-fatigue-015.question: Fatigue crack growth in a steel plate is described by the Paris law da/dN = C(ΔK)ᵐ (C = 1.0×10⁻¹², with da/dN in m/cycle, ΔK in MPa·√m, and m = 4), and ΔK = Δσ√(πa) (geometry factor 1). Under cycling with a stress range Δσ = 200 MPa, which value is closest to the number of cycles for the crack to grow from 1.0 mm to 5.0 mm? Assume that ΔK over this range (about 11–25 MPa·√m) is well above the threshold and within the range where the Paris law holds.
choices: About 2.5×10⁵ cycles
About 5.1×10⁴ cycles
About 6.3×10⁴ cycles
fracture-fatigue-015.explanation: For m = 4, da/dN = C(Δσ√π)⁴a², so separating variables and integrating gives N = (1/a₀ − 1/a_f)/[C(Δσ√π)⁴]. C(Δσ√π)⁴ = 1.0×10⁻¹²×200⁴×π² ≈ 1.58×10⁻² m⁻¹ and 1/a₀ − 1/a_f = 1000 − 200 = 800 m⁻¹, so N ≈ 800/(1.58×10⁻²) ≈ 5.1×10⁴ cycles. About 2.5×10⁵ cycles assumes the rate at the initial 1.0 mm, 1.58×10⁻⁸ m/cycle, continues to the end, ignoring that ΔK rises and the crack accelerates as it grows. About 6.3×10⁴ cycles drops the 1/a_f term. Most of the life is spent while the crack is still short, early on.

fracture-fatigue-016.question: The critical energy release rate for fracture of a steel is G_c = 20 kJ/m². Using the plane-stress relation G = K²/E with a Young's modulus E = 200 GPa, which is closest to the fracture toughness K_c?
choices: About 89 MPa·√m
About 2.0 MPa·√m
About 63 MPa·√m
fracture-fatigue-016.explanation: K_c = √(EG_c) = √(200×10⁹ × 20×10³) = √(4.0×10¹⁵) ≈ 6.3×10⁷ Pa·√m, or about 63 MPa·√m. G is the energy released per unit area of crack advance and K is the intensity of the crack-tip stress field; in linear elasticity this relation converts one into the other. About 89 MPa·√m wrongly inserts a factor of 2, as in G = K²/(2E), and about 2.0 MPa·√m leaves kJ/m² unconverted to J/m² and calculates with 20. In plane strain G = K²(1 − ν²)/E, so with ν = 0.3 the K found from the same G_c is about 5% larger. In materials such as glass, whose G_c is a few J/m², K_c is only about 1 MPa·√m.

fracture-fatigue-017.question: A round steel bar with a fully reversed fatigue limit σw = 300 MPa has a notch with a stress concentration factor Kt = 3.0. If the notch sensitivity of this steel is q = (Kf − 1)/(Kt − 1) = 0.80, which is closest to the fatigue limit of the notched bar (as nominal stress), σw/Kf? Kf is the fatigue notch factor.
choices: About 100 MPa
About 115 MPa
About 125 MPa
fracture-fatigue-017.explanation: Kf = 1 + q(Kt − 1) = 1 + 0.80 × 2.0 = 2.6, so the fatigue limit is 300/2.6 ≈ 115 MPa. In fatigue the stress falls off steeply from the notch root, and crack initiation and early growth involve the stress over a certain volume, so the actual strength reduction Kf is smaller than the elastic theoretical value Kt. q measures this: 0 means the notch has no effect and 1 means Kf = Kt. About 100 MPa takes q = 1 and divides by Kt, a conservative but low estimate. About 125 MPa calculates Kf as q × Kt = 2.4. q approaches 1 for higher-strength steels and larger notch-root radii, so controlling notch geometry is especially important in high-strength materials.

fracture-fatigue-018.question: In a highly ductile steel, when the crack-tip plastic zone spreads far relative to the plate thickness and crack length, so that fracture cannot be assessed with the linear elastic stress intensity factor K, which pair of parameters is used?
choices: The J-integral and the crack-tip opening displacement (CTOD)
The stress concentration factor Kt and the nominal stress at the notch root
The coefficient C and exponent m of the Paris law for fatigue crack growth
fracture-fatigue-018.explanation: Assessment by K holds under small-scale yielding, when the plastic zone is much smaller than the crack length and plate thickness. When the plastic zone spreads widely in a highly ductile material, this assumption breaks down. The J-integral, an integral along a path surrounding the crack tip that expresses the intensity of crack-tip deformation even in elastic-plastic materials, and the crack-tip opening displacement (CTOD), which measures how far the crack tip opens by plastic deformation, are used instead. In the linear elastic range J equals the energy release rate G, with J = K²/E′ (E′ being E or E/(1 − ν²)). The stress concentration factor is a guide to the elastic stress at a rounded notch and cannot assess a sharp crack. The Paris-law constants describe fatigue crack growth rate and are not criteria for fracture.

fracture-fatigue-019.question: A fatigue crack growing under constant amplitude receives a single large tensile overload, after which the original amplitude is restored. Which statement about the subsequent crack growth is correct?
choices: The overload sharpens and embrittles the crack tip by work hardening, so subsequent crack growth speeds up and never returns to the rate it had before the overload
No effect of the overload remains, and the original growth rate resumes from the very next cycle
Compressive residual stress remains in the large plastic zone created by the overload, the crack closes more easily, and growth is retarded for a while
fracture-fatigue-019.explanation: A tensile overload creates a crack-tip plastic zone larger than usual. On unloading, this zone is pushed back by the surrounding elastic material and is left under compressive residual stress, and as the crack grows the plastically deformed material remains on the crack faces, making the crack close more easily (crack closure). The effective stress intensity range is therefore reduced, and growth is retarded until the crack passes through the overload plastic zone. This is called overload retardation. As a result, the loading sequence affects life under variable loading, and life cannot be estimated simply by adding up the damage of each cycle. Statements that no effect remains, or that growth stays faster afterward, do not fit this observation. An overload that is too large, however, may cause fracture on the spot.

fracture-fatigue-020.question: Which is the correct way of thinking when designing a pressure vessel or pipe so that 'leak before break' holds?
choices: Make the wall thick enough that even a crack running all the way through it causes no leak, keeping the internal fluid and pressure from escaping to the outside
The length of a through-wall crack is shorter than the critical crack length at that stress, so it can be detected as a leak before unstable fracture
The fracture toughness is low, so once a crack forms the whole part breaks at once, and the part can be replaced before any crack is found
fracture-fatigue-020.explanation: A crack that grows by fatigue or stress corrosion, from the inner surface of the wall for example, eventually penetrates the wall and the fluid leaks out. If the length of the through-wall crack is then well below the critical crack length set by the service stress and fracture toughness, the vessel does not burst suddenly, and there is time to detect the leak and stop operation. This is the leak-before-break concept; it holds more readily for materials of higher fracture toughness and at lower stresses. It is not a design to prevent leaks but one that uses a leak as a safe warning. If the toughness is low and the crack reaches the critical length before penetrating, bursting occurs before any leak, which is dangerous. It is used, combined with inspection, to assess the safety of piping in nuclear and chemical plants and similar facilities.

fracture-fatigue-021.question: Under small-scale yielding, the crack tip opening displacement (CTOD) δ is related to the stress intensity factor K by δ = K²/(mσyE), where m is a constraint factor of about 1 to 2. For a steel with yield stress σy = 500 MPa and Young's modulus E = 200 GPa, with K = 100 MPa·√m and m = 1, what is δ?
choices: About 40 mm
About 0.10 mm
About 0.050 mm
fracture-fatigue-021.explanation: δ = K²/(mσyE) = (100×10⁶)²/(1 × 500×10⁶ × 200×10⁹) = 1.0×10¹⁶/1.0×10²⁰ = 1.0×10⁻⁴ m, about 0.10 mm. Using G = K²/E, this can also be written δ = G/(mσy), showing that the energy to advance the crack is expressed as the product of the opening and the yield stress. About 40 mm omits E and computes (K/σy)², confusing CTOD with the formula for estimating plastic zone size. About 0.050 mm uses m = 2, assuming highly constrained plane strain, which does not match the stated m = 1. Because CTOD can be measured even in highly ductile steels whose large plastic zones prevent assessment by K, it is used to assess the fracture toughness of welded structures.

fracture-fatigue-022.question: Studies of fatigue crack growth show that short cracks (microstructurally small cracks), no longer than a few grain diameters, can grow at ΔK values below the threshold ΔK_th measured on long cracks, and their growth rates scatter widely. What is the main reason?
choices: In short cracks, closure by the crack faces touching has not yet developed, and grain orientation and boundaries act on them directly
Short cracks still have blunt tips, so the stress concentration at the tip is stronger than for long cracks, and they grow faster than long cracks at the same ΔK
Short cracks lie at the surface, where air oxidizes the tip and the oxide wedges the crack open, so they grow even at low ΔK
fracture-fatigue-022.explanation: In long cracks, the plastically deformed material left behind the tip, the roughness of the fracture surfaces and oxides make the crack faces touch and close early (crack closure), so the ΔK actually driving the tip is smaller than the nominal value. In a short crack this closure has not yet built up, so at the same nominal ΔK the effective driving force is larger, and the crack grows even below ΔK_th. Moreover, when a crack spans only a few grains, its ease of growth depends on grain orientation and it may stop at grain boundaries, so the scatter is large. A blunt tip actually weakens the stress concentration. Oxide wedging increases closure and slows growth, so it cannot explain why short cracks grow more easily.

fracture-fatigue-023.question: Fatigue damage is to be estimated with Miner's rule from a record of irregularly varying load. What is the main reason for using a cycle-counting method such as rainflow counting?
choices: It separates small reversals superimposed on larger swings and counts each closed hysteresis loop by its amplitude and mean stress
Damage is fixed by the number of load peaks alone, so a method is needed to count peaks quickly without regard to amplitude
Mean stress effects vanish under irregular loading, so every swing can be replaced by a constant amplitude equal to half the difference between the maximum and minimum
fracture-fatigue-023.explanation: Real component loads are complex waveforms in which small fluctuations ride on larger ones. Rainflow counting extracts a cycle each time, in the sequence of load maxima and minima, a swing returns to the value at which it started, so after the small reversals are counted, the larger swing enclosing them is kept as one large cycle. Cycles counted this way correspond to closed hysteresis loops on the stress-strain diagram, and the damage from each, based on its amplitude and mean stress, is summed with Miner's rule. Counting peaks alone cannot distinguish the large amplitudes that dominate damage. Mean stress effects remain under irregular loading, and replacing everything with one constant amplitude from the overall maximum and minimum greatly misjudges the damage.

fracture-fatigue-024.question: It is known that raising the tensile strength of the parent steel hardly improves the fatigue strength of welded steel joints. What is the main reason?
choices: The stronger the steel, the more the weld heat softens the heat-affected zone, so joint strength is set only by the softened zone, regardless of parent strength
Toe stress concentration, small flaws and tensile residual stress near yield make initiation almost immediate, so life is set mostly by crack growth
Welded joints are loaded above the yield stress, so they always undergo low-cycle fatigue, and life is set only by ductility, not by strength
fracture-fatigue-024.explanation: At the weld toe the geometry changes abruptly and stress concentrates, and small flaws such as undercut and slag entrapment are present from the start. Cooling after welding also leaves tensile residual stress close to the yield stress, so almost no life is spent on crack initiation and crack growth occupies most of it. The fatigue crack growth rate in steels is largely insensitive to tensile strength, so a stronger parent metal does little to extend joint life. Welded joint design therefore uses relationships between stress range and life that do not depend on steel strength, and usually omits the mean stress correction because of the residual stress. Improvements come from treatments such as smoothing the weld toe.

fracture-fatigue-025.question: When round bars are twisted to fracture, ductile metals break almost flat on a plane perpendicular to the axis, whereas brittle materials such as gray cast iron or chalk crack along a helical surface at about 45° to the axis. Why do brittle materials fail in a helix?
choices: Brittle materials are weak in shear, so they slide apart along the plane at 45° to the axis on which the maximum shear stress acts
The torsional shear stress is larger at the center than at the surface, so a crack starting at the center spreads outward at an angle into a helix
In pure shear the maximum tensile principal stress acts at 45° to the axis, and brittle materials crack normal to it
fracture-fatigue-025.explanation: In torsion of a round bar, a surface element is in pure shear, and the shear stress is greatest on planes perpendicular and parallel to the axis. Rotating this state by 45° gives tensile and compressive principal stresses, each equal in magnitude to the shear stress, at ±45° to the axis. Ductile metals yield and part in shear, so they fracture flat on the plane perpendicular to the axis, which is a plane of maximum shear stress. Brittle materials are weak in tension and crack on the plane perpendicular to the maximum tensile principal stress, which winds around the axis as a 45° helix. The planes of maximum shear stress are not at 45°, so attributing the helix to shear failure is wrong. The shear stress is proportional to the distance from the center and is largest at the surface, not the center.
